title: Chicken Cacciatore
subtitle: Italian-American braised chicken with peppers and tomato
excerpt: Chicken cacciatore is a braised chicken dish of Italian-American cooking: bone-in pieces cooked with onions, peppers, tinned tomatoes, and a little wine until the sauce is thick and the chicken is tender enough to fall from the bone.
sourceNotes: Chicken cacciatore (hunter's chicken) exists in both Italian and Italian-American versions. The Italian-American version, common in New York Italian restaurants, tends to use bell peppers and more tomato than the Italian original. This follows the Italian-American style.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions with sauce. Reheat gently in a covered pan.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The flavour improves overnight. Cool, refrigerate, and reheat gently over low heat.

content.text: Chicken cacciatore is a braise: bone-in chicken pieces seared and then simmered in a sauce of onion, peppers, garlic, tinned tomatoes, and white wine until the sauce has reduced to something thick and the chicken has given up all its juices to it. The name means hunter's chicken, referring to the kind of rustic, catch-what-you-can cooking that uses vegetables and wine with whatever meat is available. It serves four from one pot and takes under an hour.

Pat {{chicken-thigh}} dry with kitchen paper and season generously. Heat {{olive-oil}} in a large heavy-based pan or casserole over medium-high heat. Sear the chicken skin side down for five to six minutes until the skin is deep golden. Turn and sear the other side for three minutes. Remove and set aside.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add {{onion}} to the same pan and cook for five minutes until softened. Add {{pepper-red}}, {{pepper-green}}, and {{garlic}}. Cook for another five minutes until the peppers are beginning to soften.

Pour in {{dry-white-wine}} and scrape up any browned bits from the base. Allow to bubble for two minutes. Add {{tinned-tomatoes}}, {{chicken-stock}}, {{oregano-dried}}, and {{bay-leaves}}. Season with salt and pepper.

Return the chicken skin side up to the pan, nestling the pieces into the sauce. The liquid should come halfway up the sides of the chicken. Reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid slightly ajar, and simmer for 30 to 35 minutes until the chicken is cooked through.
Remove the lid for the last ten minutes to thicken the sauce. Discard the bay leaves. Stir in {{olives-black}} if using and scatter with {{parsley-flat}}. Serve with bread, polenta, or pasta.

items.symptom: The skin is pale and flabby after braising
items.cause: The skin softens once it's braised in liquid.
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final ten minutes to help the skin firm up. Alternatively, after braising, transfer the chicken briefly to a hot grill for two minutes to re-crisp the skin before serving.

items.symptom: The sauce is thin and watery
items.cause: Lid on too tight throughout, or not enough simmering time.
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for an additional ten minutes to reduce. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.

items.symptom: The chicken is tough and stringy
items.cause: Thighs are forgiving but still need at least 30 minutes at a gentle simmer.
items.fix: Check the liquid: it should be at a steady, gentle bubble throughout. Too fierce and the chicken toughens; too low and it steams rather than braises.

items.cause: Insufficient seasoning, or not enough fond from the searing step.
items.fix: Season the chicken generously before searing. Make sure the searing step produces a deep golden crust: the browned bits dissolve into the sauce and are where a lot of the flavour comes from.

content.text: Cacciatore means hunter in Italian, and the dish appears across Italian regional cooking. The Italian-American version is more generously sauced than the original. Bell peppers are central. They became a marker of Italian-American cooking because they were cheap and abundant. The dish became a staple of neighbourhood restaurants in New York and New Jersey.
